summary: An excerpt from a novel (Book 4, part 103) set in a futuristic city after a revolution that freed a nation from imperial European powers. The narrator, Valentine, a thirteen-year-old girl, spends the day at a newly built cinema across from her apartment building, describing a series of marvels the city has recently built, from flying cars to robot insect factories. She recalls the revolution from childhood, marked by hunger, grey dirt, and tension at home, and the excerpt ends with her finding the cinema's films dull because they dwell on the revolution.
one_line: Thirteen-year-old Valentine spends a day at a marvelous new cinema in a post-revolution city, remembering the hardship of the revolution.
key_facts: The narrator's city was shaped by a revolution that liberated it from imperial European powers, and its revolutionaries kept their GDP at home to become an industrial powerhouse.
The day the siege began, Valentine was at the cinema across the street from her building.
The cinema had grown the night before, with gossamer silver supports and candy-apple red curves.
Valentine begged her parents, Mata and Popa, to let her go to the cinema.
The week before the cinema, the city had clever little flying cars that swooped past each other with millimeters to spare.
Before the flying cars, the city had a candy forest where trees sprouted bon-bons and sticks of rock.
Robot insect swarms gathered litter and dust and turned it into brightly colored factories at the edge of town.
Valentine was ten years old during the revolution and is now thirteen.
Valentine remembers being always a little hungry, and her parents whispering angrily at each other during the revolution.
Her little brother Trover cried thin sickly cries all night during the revolution.
Valentine and the other little girls tinkered with a balcony's controls until it lifted free and sailed to a spot under the dome.
From the balcony, the screen was a little distorted, but the viewers could count the bald spots on the old war heroes' heads.
Airborne robots silently intercepted the spitballs the boys threw so they did not disturb other watchers.
Valentine thinks the films are not very good because the first one is all about the revolution, which is all the children talk about in school.
